content: Maternal death, also referred to as maternal mortality or obstetrical death, is defined as the death of a woman during pregnancy or within a short period after the pregnancy ends. In 2000, the United Nations estimated that there were approximately 529,000 maternal deaths globally, with less than 1% occurring in developed countries. Despite this, the majority of these deaths have been preventable for decades, as effective medical interventions to address the causes of maternal mortality have been available since the 1950s. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines maternal death as the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of the termination of pregnancy, regardless of the pregnancy's duration or location, due to causes related to or worsened by the pregnancy or its management. This definition excludes deaths caused by accidental or incidental factors. Maternal deaths are categorized as either direct or indirect. Direct maternal deaths result from complications of pregnancy, delivery, or their management. Indirect maternal deaths occur in women with preexisting or newly developed health conditions that are exacerbated by pregnancy. Deaths unrelated to pregnancy, such as those caused by accidents or incidental factors, are classified as non-obstetrical maternal deaths. Maternal mortality is considered a critical indicator of the quality of a healthcare system. However, it is important to note that the WHO definition is not the only one in use. Some definitions include deaths from accidental or incidental causes, such as violence against women, which may be influenced by the pregnancy and the surrounding socioeconomic and cultural environment. Additionally, approximately 10% of maternal deaths occur after the 42-day postpartum period, leading some definitions to extend the observation period to one year after the end of pregnancy. It is also widely recognized that maternal mortality statistics are often underreported. The primary causes of maternal death include bacterial infections, toxemia, obstetrical hemorrhage, ectopic pregnancy, puerperal sepsis, amniotic fluid embolism, and complications from abortion. According to the 2005 WHO report Make Every Mother and Child Count, the leading causes of maternal death are severe bleeding or hemorrhage (25%), infections (13%), eclampsia (12%), obstructed labor (8%), complications from abortion (13%), other direct causes (8%), and indirect causes (20%). Indirect causes include conditions such as malaria, anemia, HIV/AIDS, and cardiovascular disease, which can complicate pregnancy or be worsened by it. Severe cases of hyperemesis gravidarum can also result in maternal death. This ratio serves as an indicator of the quality of a healthcare system. In 2000, Sierra Leone had the highest maternal mortality ratio at 2,000 deaths per 100,000 live births, followed by Afghanistan at 1,900. In contrast, countries like Iceland and Austria had some of the lowest ratios, with 0 and 4 deaths per 100,000 live births, respectively. In the United States, the maternal mortality ratio was 17 per 100,000 live births in 2000. The lifetime risk of maternal death considers both the number of pregnancies a woman has and the associated risks. For example, in sub-Saharan Africa, the lifetime risk of maternal death is 1 in 16, compared to 1 in 2,800 in developed nations. A 2003 report by WHO, UNICEF, and UNFPA, based on data from 2000, found that the global average maternal mortality ratio was 400 per 100,000 live births, with developed regions averaging 20 and developing regions averaging 440. The countries with the highest ratios included Sierra Leone (2,000), Afghanistan (1,900), and Malawi (1,800), among others. It is important to note that the term Maternal Mortality Rate is often used interchangeably with Maternal Mortality Ratio, but this is technically incorrect. The MMR is a ratio, not a rate. High maternal mortality rates are often observed in countries with high infant mortality rates, reflecting poor overall nutrition and inadequate medical care. Low birth weight in infants is associated with an increased risk of maternal death due to cardiovascular complications. For every pound decrease in infant birth weight, the risk of maternal death doubles. Conversely, higher infant birth weights are associated with a lower risk of maternal death. In the 20th century, maternal death rates declined dramatically. At the beginning of the century, maternal mortality was approximately 1 in 100 live births. By the year 2000, this figure had decreased significantly, with the maternal mortality ratio in the United States being 13 per 100,000 live births—a reduction by a factor of 100. This decline is largely attributed to advancements in aseptic techniques, the increased use of cesarean sections, improved fluid management and blood transfusion practices, and better prenatal care.
